cita: Omri et al. (2026). Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads.
problema: Agent memory systems (flat retrieval, LLM-mediated extraction, consolidating fact stores, agentic control flows) are evaluated only on downstream accuracy, leaving their system-level cost behavior (construction vs retrieval vs generation) entirely uncharacterized despite drastically and asymmetrically redistributing compute cost across the write and read paths.
mecanismo: A four-axis taxonomy (construction, storage, retrieval, mutability) classifies 10 representative systems into 4 paradigms (long-context, flat RAG, structure-augmented RAG [append-only/consolidating], agentic control flow); a phase-aware profiling harness attributes API telemetry (tokens, calls) and hardware telemetry (GPU utilization, VRAM, HBM bandwidth, energy) to construction, retrieval, and generation phases on the same monotonic timeline.
evaluacion: MemoryAgentBench (4 competencies: accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, selective forgetting) + MemoryArena (multi-session freshness-latency); measured on LongMemEval_S_* (5 samples ~360K tokens history, 300 queries) under remote (OpenAI API) and local (vLLM on H100) construction regimes across an LLM ladder (Qwen3-32B/14B/8B/1.7B).
numeros_clave: Table3 (Qwen3-32B, 300 queries): accuracy ranges 20.0% (MIRIX) to 47.0% (BM25); end-to-end energy spans 26.7x, from BM25's 582 kJ to Letta's 15,429 kJ; per-correct-answer energy from BM25's 4,128 J floor to A-Mem 116,116 J and MIRIX 144,629 J (28-47x premium). Fig.2: Mem0 answers a query in <0.1s vs ~38s for a long-context (GPT-4.1-mini) baseline.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's central contribution is a measured cost taxonomy (Table3, Fig.3/4: tokens, GPU energy, latency per phase) showing costs invisible to accuracy metrics span 26.7x in energy and 2 orders of magnitude in per-query latency, directly confirming MF's stance that context economy must be measured per design choice, not assumed.

The paper documents that 'maintenance is weak or absent' in most current systems -- memory accumulates indefinitely with no freshness/pruning policy (S2.1) -- an explicit gap MF's own forgetting/negative-knowledge design should not repeat.

Table 1's taxonomy shows storage substrates range from a single raw-context buffer to multi-store DBs coupling lexical/vector/graph/structured metadata (MIRIX, Letta) -- directly informing MF's single-store-vs-multi-store seam tradeoff with a measured cost consequence.

Fig.2 explicitly measures per-query retrieval+generation latency and accuracy jointly across 10 systems rather than reporting accuracy alone, confirming MF's stance that retrieval must be measured (cost AND quality) not assumed.

notes: Table 1 taxonomy + Table 3 end-to-end cost + Fig.2-4 (phase breakdown, energy-per-correct-answer), arXiv 2606.06448 (Stanford/MIT/KU Leuven).

cita: Asawa et al. (2026). Continual Learning Bench: Evaluating Frontier AI Systems in Real-World Stateful Environments.
problema: No high-quality benchmark exists to measure whether AI systems genuinely improve through sequential online experience (continual learning), distinct from recall/QA benchmarks; existing memory evaluations conflate learning with static base-model capability.
mecanismo: CL-Bench: 6 expert-validated domains with discoverable latent structure (schema conventions, opponent strategies, codebase layout) shared across sequential instances, some with concept drift requiring re-learning; introduces a 'gain' metric (gt = r_sf_t - r_sl_t, stateful minus stateless reward on the SAME instance) to isolate the causal contribution of accumulated state from base capability, plus cross-task normalization against an external stateless reference.
evaluacion: Frontier models (Claude Opus 4.7/Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro/3 Flash, GPT-5.4) x continual-learning systems (full-context ICL, ICL Notepad, Mem0, ACE playbook, Claude Code, Codex) averaged over 5 rollouts/task; measures normalized reward, normalized gain, and USD cost per system.
numeros_clave: Table1: full-context ICL+Sonnet4.6 ranks #1 (22.3% norm. reward, 25.4% norm. gain, $30.4/run); ACE (dedicated memory playbook) ranks 9th by gain (8.6%) despite the highest cost ($62.8/run); Mem0+GPT-5.4 ranks 4th (15.1% reward, 20.2% gain, $18.3). Naive ICL occupies 3 of the top 5 ranks by gain.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Central finding is that dedicated memory-management systems (Mem0, ACE) underperform naive full-context ICL on the gain metric (Table1) despite far higher cost, directly challenging any MF assumption that adding an explicit memory/consolidation layer necessarily improves online learning over just keeping context.

The gain-vs-cost figure plots normalized gain against USD cost per system and shows ACE's $62.8/run buys LESS gain than $30.4 ICL, confirming MF's stance that memory-architecture cost must be measured against the gain it actually produces, not assumed proportional.

The gain metric (S4.2, gt=r_sf-r_sl on the SAME instance) is a rigorous measured-memory-value construction MF could adopt directly: it isolates the causal contribution of accumulated state from base-model capability, rather than reporting raw accuracy.

The Database Exploration task's concept-drift variant (Fig.1, a schema migration mid-task) explicitly tests whether a system detects and discards STALE past experience rather than blindly reusing it, confirming MF's fidelity/staleness concern is a real, measured failure mode (frontier systems are shown 'rigid in early, incorrect beliefs').

notes: Table 1 rankings + Fig.5 learning curves + Fig.1 Database Exploration concept-drift illustration, arXiv 2606.05661 (Berkeley/Snorkel AI/Wisconsin).

cita: Biswas (2026). COMA: Adaptive Context Budget Management for Memory-Augmented RAG via Query-Aware Zone Allocation, Memory-Conditioned Retrieval, and Cognitive Memory Consolidation.
problema: RAG systems treat context assembly as concatenate-then-truncate with no allocation policy across competing zones (system prompt, working memory, retrieval, episodic history, scratchpad); retrieval is conditioned only on the query, ignoring what the agent already knows; and memory management (promotion/eviction/decay) relies on hand-crafted rules that cannot adapt.
mecanismo: COMA combines (1) a Query-Aware Context Budget Allocator that partitions the token budget across 5 zones via calibrated heuristic profiles conditioned on query complexity/task type/memory state (with a pluggable neural-replacement interface); (2) a Memory-Conditioned Retriever extending Maximal Marginal Relevance to penalize candidates already covered by working memory (score = rel(c,q)*(1-lambda*max cos(c,m))); (3) a Three-Tier Cognitive Memory (sensory/working/long-term) with Ebbinghaus-inspired exponential-decay retention and a 4-operation consolidation engine (extract/consolidate/merge/decay-sweep).
evaluacion: GPT-4.1-mini vs naive-RAG/fixed-allocation/no-memory ablations on (i) a real 10-paper research corpus with LLM-as-judge scoring (relevance/groundedness/completeness/conciseness/recall) and (ii) 3 synthetic multi-turn scenarios (20 turns, 50 docs, planted facts) using 4 new metrics (ContextWaste, MemoryRecall@K, RedundancyScore, ContextEfficiency).
numeros_clave: Real-corpus (Table IV): COMA uses 99,585 tokens vs Naive RAG's 158,233 (37.1% reduction), recall accuracy 1.000 vs 0.500, relevance 0.923 vs 0.910, but lower groundedness 0.464 vs 0.687. Synthetic (Table V): ContextEfficiency 3.725-4.031 vs 0.738-0.747 for Naive RAG (5.4x gain); MemoryRecall@20 = 1.000 vs 0.000 for memory-less baselines; ContextWaste 0.489-0.493 vs 0.650 (24.2% reduction).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's central measured result is a budget-allocation policy across 5 competing context zones (Table I) that cuts real-corpus token usage by 37.1% while improving recall (Table IV), confirming MF's stance that context economy across write/retrieve/scratch zones is a first-class, measurable design axis.

The Memory-Conditioned Retriever (Eq.1) penalizes retrieving chunks ALREADY covered by working memory, an explicit 'don't re-fetch what you already know' negative-knowledge filter that directly reduces token waste (RedundancyScore), a pattern MF's retrieval layer could adopt.

The four-operation consolidation engine (Extract/Consolidate/Merge/Decay-sweep, S3.E) with an explicit similarity-threshold merge step (mu=0.85) that prevents 'semantic fragmentation over long conversations' is a concrete, parameterized promotion-to-durable-memory mechanism MF's own consolidation design could mirror.

The paper's own honest limitation (S6) that COMA's lower groundedness score reflects a judge-protocol mismatch (penalizing correct memory-sourced citations as ungrounded) is a cautionary note for MF about how retrieval/fidelity evaluation harnesses must account for cross-turn provenance, not just single-turn chunk citation.

notes: Table I allocation profiles + Table IV real-corpus results + Table V synthetic benchmark + S3.E consolidation engine, single-author preprint (IIT Kharagpur), Harvard Dataverse release.

cita: Chen and Cheng (2026). Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory.
problema: Forgetting/consolidation decisions in agentic memory are made at consolidation time, BEFORE the future query is known, yet production systems rank memories by query-similarity (a retrieval-time signal) or recency, both mis-specified for the governing triage decision of what to keep under a fixed memory budget.
mecanismo: A learned multi-factor value V(m)=sum(wi*fi(m)) over 7 cognitive-psychology-grounded factors (emotional intensity, goal relevance, value alignment, self/user relevance, task utility, reliability, usage history); weights are fit by a gradient-free hill-climb optimizer against a downstream objective (gold-evidence retention). The single scalar V(m) uniformly drives encoding depth (4 tiers), a forget score (age and retrieval-count combined with a 1/V(m) resistance term), and retrieval rank, replacing three separately hand-tuned rules. The key methodological move separates 'oracle' goal-relevance (computed against the held-out future query, measuring retrieval) from 'blind' goal-relevance (a query-agnostic session-topic centroid, measuring true forgetting).
evaluacion: A synthetic confound study (60 train/60 test cases with planted value-alignment/self-relevance confounds) plus real LongMemEval-S (479/500 usable cases, oracle vs blind regimes, keep-fraction sweep kappa in [0.1,0.5]) vs uniform-weight/single-factor/recency baselines; an MLP ablation over the same factors tests linear vs nonlinear capacity; all experiments CPU-only, no API calls.
numeros_clave: LongMemEval blind regime (keep 30%, 479 cases): learned multi-factor value retains 0.770+/-0.011 gold evidence vs uniform 0.657, best single factor (self-relevance) 0.518, recency 0.368, goal-only 0.286 (near 0.30 chance floor); oracle regime saturates at 0.993 (goal-only alone reaches 0.979), exposing the retrieval-vs-forgetting metric artifact. Synthetic confound study: learned weighting retains 1.00 vs uniform 0.62, single-factor policies 0.00.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's central methodological claim is that scoring goal-relevance against the FUTURE evaluation question ('oracle') saturates retention (~0.98) and looks like a forgetting win, but this 'measures retrieval, not forgetting' -- directly challenging any MF benchmark that scores its own forgetting/consolidation policy using knowledge unavailable at write time.

A single learned scalar V(m) drives encoding depth, forget-risk, AND retrieval rank (fig.1, S3.2) replacing three separately-tuned rules, a unifying write/forget/retrieve trigger design MF's own memory gate could adopt instead of independent heuristics per operation.

Table1's 'reliability' factor (provenance heuristic: user-stated > model-stated) is learned to carry the largest weight (0.64) in the blind regime on real data, empirically confirming MF's provenance/fidelity concern is a measurably dominant signal for what should durably survive consolidation.

The entire evaluation reproduces CPU-only with zero API calls (S6, local sentence-transformer embeddings + gradient-free optimizer over 7 scalars), a concrete demonstration that a useful memory-value signal need not cost an LLM call per item, confirming MF's economy-of-context stance.

notes: Table 3 oracle-vs-blind LongMemEval results + Fig.2/3 + Table 2 synthetic confound study, arXiv 2606.12945 v2.

cita: Liu et al. (2026). StreamMemBench: Streaming Evaluation of Agent Memory for Future-Oriented Assistance.
problema: Existing memory benchmarks test dialogue recall or task-behavior improvement in isolation using synthetic/scripted evidence, leaving untested the full streaming trajectory from real egocentric observations to evidence use in an initial task, feedback incorporation, and follow-up reuse in a later related task.
mecanismo: StreamMemBench builds evidence anchors from EgoLife egocentric lifelog segments (an anchor agent extracts user-specific evidence plus two task queries per anchor; a review agent filters for no-leak/necessity/naturalness); evaluation runs a chronological trajectory (initial task -> response -> user feedback -> post-feedback response -> memory commit -> follow-up task -> response) scored by four metrics: Fidelity (evidence preserved in the memory delta), Initial Evidence Use (IEU), Feedback Incorporation (FI), Follow-up Reuse (FUR).
evaluacion: 2 retrieval baselines (RAGraw, RAGext) + 6 memory systems (Mem0, EverMemOS, A-Mem, MemOS, MemoryOS, MemSkill) x 2 backbones (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini-3-Flash) on 8,107 evidence anchors / 16,214 queries from 3,347 EgoLife segments; temporal-drift analysis across stream position (early/mid/late); a 5-way lifecycle-failure taxonomy; storage/latency/token-cost measurement per segment.
numeros_clave: Table2 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash): A-Mem's highest FUR is 64.98 with 100% Fidelity; MemOS has high FI (77.25) but near-collapsed FUR (2.94) despite 67.97 Fidelity -- a large Fidelity-minus-FUR gap. Table3 per-segment cost: compact systems (EverMemOS 502B, Mem0 569B, MemOS 658B) vs raw/linked (RAGraw 8044B, MemoryOS 8286B); token cost ranges 5.34k (RAGext) to 38.57k (A-Mem)/38.48k (MemoryOS).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Evidence anchors explicitly retain 'a long-term preference, plan, commitment or capability' (S3.1) and generate activity-planning-type task queries, confirming plan-state is one of the first-class memory contents whose future reuse this benchmark measures, directly relevant to MF's plan-state-as-memory need.

The 5-way lifecycle-failure taxonomy (Formation/Initial-use/Feedback-incorporation/Correction-consolidation/Evidence-use-persistence failure, Fig.4) is a concrete template for diagnosing WHERE a memory pipeline silently drops information, a negative-knowledge-style failure attribution MF's own memory gate could adopt.

The central finding -- 'systems with perfect or high Fidelity can still have much lower IEU and FUR' (S4.2), e.g. MemOS 67.97 Fidelity but 2.94 FUR -- directly confirms MF's fidelity concern that storage/retention alone does not guarantee correct future use, a distinct failure mode from staleness or poisoning.

Table3 shows storage, latency, and token cost do NOT move together (e.g. A-Mem is token-expensive at 38.57k/segment despite moderate latency), confirming MF's stance that context economy must be measured on multiple independent axes, not a single proxy.

notes: Table 2 main results + Table 3 storage/latency/token cost + Fig.3 temporal-drift curves + Fig.4 failure taxonomy, arXiv 2606.14571.

cita: Long et al. (2026). MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory.
problema: Memory benchmarks aggregate accuracy over independent question rows/episodes, hiding how a SINGLE fact behaves as conditions change (aging, question type, evidence present/missing/conflicting); pooled scores cannot show that a system answering a fact's current state correctly may still fail on its trajectory or under a false premise.
mecanismo: MemTrace uses the 'knowledge point' (a single typed user fact) as the unit of measurement; each fact is probed along 3 controlled dimensions -- memory age (8 chronological checkpoints), question type (current/historical/trajectory), evidence condition (present/missing/conflicting) -- scored on Gist accuracy/Verbatim completeness/Response type, plus a failure-attribution protocol (oracle-with-gold-evidence vs retriever-reach-vs-use replay) distinguishing unreachable from reachable-but-unused evidence.
evaluacion: 13 memory-system configurations across 4 paradigms (long-context: Qwen3.5-35B/Gemini-3-Flash/GPT-5-nano; RAG: BM25/text-emb-3-small/Qwen3-Emb/HippoRAG-v2; external-memory: Mem0/SimpleMem/REMem/AMem; agentic: MIRIX/Mem-T) on 835 knowledge points/20 users, expanded to 15,422 question rows and 200,453 scored answers (built from HaluMem-Medium).
numeros_clave: When systems fail, gold evidence was retrievable ~10x more often than missing (dominant bottleneck = evidence USE not retrieval). Saturated trajectory Gist collapses for long-context models: Qwen3.5-35B 49.0%(fresh)->6.7%(saturated), GPT-5-nano 38.4%->6.5%. Boundary-safe systems (Mem0 99.3% boundary abstention) barely resolve conflicts (Mem0 conflict Gist 14.6%). Oracle-evidence lift on hard failure subsets: +65.6 to +85.0 percentage points (Fig.5).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's headline finding is that when systems fail, the evidence was retrievable ~10x more often than missing -- 'improving memory depends on using reachable evidence, not on more storage or retrieval' -- directly challenging any MF assumption that better retrieval/storage is the main lever, when evidence-USE is the dominant bottleneck.

The failure-attribution protocol (oracle-on-hard-failures + reach-vs-use replay, S3.4/Fig.5) is exactly a measured decomposition of retrieval-reach vs generation-use, directly confirming MF's stance that retrieval quality must be isolated and measured, not inferred from end accuracy.

Table4/Fig.4 shows boundary-safe systems (Mem0, AMem, REMem) that correctly abstain on missing evidence (94-99%) nonetheless fail to correct FALSE-PREMISE (conflict) probes (14.6-35.1% Gist), confirming MF's fidelity concern that safe abstention and active conflict-resolution are separate capabilities a memory system can have one without the other.

Trajectory questions (how a fact changed over time) require connecting MULTIPLE stored states with correct temporal order, not a single lookup (S4.2), evidence that a derived/cached index needs to preserve state history and ordering, not just the latest value, to support trajectory-style queries.

notes: Table 3 memory-maintenance by question type + Table 4 conflict/boundary profile + Fig.4/5 diagnostics, arXiv 2606.17328.
